HW5_Decomposition_Hung Jui Chao

Hung Jui Chao

2026-10-07

Decomposition

Install Package

library(readxl)
library(forecast)

Read Excel

NJ <- read_excel("NJ_Unemployment_Rate_5Y.xlsx",
                 sheet = "NJ Unemployment Data")

head(NJ)
## # A tibble: 6 × 2
##   Date                NJ_Unemployment_Rate
##   <dttm>                             <dbl>
## 1 2020-09-01 00:00:00                  7.4
## 2 2020-10-01 00:00:00                  7.1
## 3 2020-11-01 00:00:00                  7.2
## 4 2020-12-01 00:00:00                  7.3
## 5 2021-01-01 00:00:00                  7.4
## 6 2021-02-01 00:00:00                  7.4

Create monthly time series Data

NJ_ts <- ts(NJ$NJ_Unemployment_Rate, start = c(2020,9), frequency = 12)
NJ_ts
##      Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec
## 2020                                 7.4 7.1 7.2 7.3
## 2021 7.4 7.4 7.3 7.3 7.0 7.2 6.9 6.7 6.2 5.9 5.6 5.5
## 2022 5.2 4.7 4.3 4.1 3.8 3.6 3.3 3.1 3.3 3.5 3.7 3.8
## 2023 3.9 4.0 4.1 4.2 4.2 4.3 4.4 4.5 4.5 4.5 4.5 4.5
## 2024 4.5 4.5 4.5 4.6 4.6 4.6 4.7 4.7 4.7 4.7 4.8 4.8
## 2025 4.9 5.0 5.1 5.1 5.2 5.4 5.5 5.5

Plot Time series

plot(NJ_ts)

Use Stl and Plot

stl_decomp_NJ <- stl(NJ_ts,s.window ="periodic")
plot(stl_decomp_NJ)

Explain: The STL decomposition shows a clear trend in NJ unemployment rate. The unemployment rate decreased from 2021 to around 2022-2023 and then gradually increased afterward. A recurring seasonality pattern is also presented but its magnitutude is relatively small compared to overall trend which only range from -0.05 to 0.05. The remainder fluctuates around zero, representing irregular variations that cannot be explained by the trend and seasonality.

See the attribute

attributes(stl_decomp_NJ)
## $names
## [1] "time.series" "weights"     "call"        "win"         "deg"        
## [6] "jump"        "inner"       "outer"      
## 
## $class
## [1] "stl"

Do the seasonal adjustment

seas_stl_decomp_NJ <- seasadj(stl_decomp_NJ) ## remove seasonal effect
seas_stl_decomp_NJ
##           Jan      Feb      Mar      Apr      May      Jun      Jul      Aug
## 2020                                                                        
## 2021 7.322412 7.354040 7.285667 7.266427 7.047187 7.167178 6.907169 6.743030

## 2023 3.822412 3.954040 4.085667 4.166427 4.247187 4.267178 4.407169 4.543030
## 2024 4.422412 4.454040 4.485667 4.566427 4.647187 4.567178 4.707169 4.743030
## 2025 4.822412 4.954040 5.085667 5.066427 5.247187 5.367178 5.507169 5.543030

## 2020 7.450476 7.182731 7.214986 7.258699
## 2021 6.250476 5.982731 5.614986 5.458699
## 2022 3.350476 3.582731 3.714986 3.758699
## 2023 4.550476 4.582731 4.514986 4.458699
## 2024 4.750476 4.782731 4.814986 4.758699
## 2025

Plot

plot(NJ_ts)
lines(seas_stl_decomp_NJ, col = "red")

Explain: We can tell from the chart that seasonal effect to the NJ unemployment rate is relatively small since the line of NJ unemployment rate without seasonal effect is almost matched to the orginal data. This also show in the graph of stl_decomp_NJ that seasonality is relatively small compared to the overall trend which only range from -0.05 to 0.05.

Do the forecast for next year NJ unemployment rate

fc_stl_NJ <- forecast(stl_decomp_NJ, h = 12)
fc_stl_NJ
##          Point Forecast    Lo 80    Hi 80    Lo 95    Hi 95
## Sep 2025       5.544716 5.384464 5.704967 5.299632 5.789799
## Oct 2025       5.547049 5.256119 5.837980 5.102109 5.991989
## Nov 2025       5.642465 5.205922 6.079008 4.974830 6.310100

## Feb 2026       5.757425 4.875125 6.639725 4.408063 7.106787

## Apr 2026       5.765439 4.603736 6.927142 3.988768 7.542110
## May 2026       5.691933 4.398188 6.985678 3.713321 7.670545
## Jun 2026       5.777745 4.357168 7.198321 3.605161 7.950329
## Jul 2026       5.742396 4.200072 7.284720 3.383615 8.101177
## Aug 2026       5.710249 4.051052 7.369447 3.172725 8.247774

Plot the forecast

plot(fc_stl_NJ)

Explain: ETS(A,Ad,N) forecasts the future one year series using an additive error and damped trend. A means additive Error, Ad means Additive Dampend Trend, and N means No Seansonality in the ETS component.

Use other option to do the decomposition: decompose()

decomp_NJ <- decompose(NJ_ts)

See the attributes

attributes(decomp_NJ)
## $names
## [1] "x"        "seasonal" "trend"    "random"   "figure"   "type"    
## 
## $class
## [1] "decomposed.ts"

Remove Seasonal from decomp_NJ

seasadj_decomp_NJ = seasadj(decomp_NJ)
seasadj_decomp_NJ
##           Jan      Feb      Mar      Apr      May      Jun      Jul      Aug
## 2020                                                                        
## 2021 7.353733 7.401649 7.292274 7.239149 7.039149 7.163108 6.911024 6.734983
## 2022 5.153733 4.701649 4.292274 4.039149 3.839149 3.563108 3.311024 3.134983
## 2023 3.853733 4.001649 4.092274 4.139149 4.239149 4.263108 4.411024 4.534983
## 2024 4.453733 4.501649 4.492274 4.539149 4.639149 4.563108 4.711024 4.734983
## 2025 4.853733 5.001649 5.092274 5.039149 5.239149 5.363108 5.511024 5.534983
##           Sep      Oct      Nov      Dec
## 2020 7.462066 7.141233 7.199566 7.262066
## 2021 6.262066 5.941233 5.599566 5.462066
## 2022 3.362066 3.541233 3.699566 3.762066
## 2023 4.562066 4.541233 4.499566 4.462066
## 2024 4.762066 4.741233 4.799566 4.762066
## 2025

Explain: We can see from the result the seasonal effect has been removed. Take Jun 2021 for example, original data is 7.4 with trend:NA, seasonality: 0.0462673611, random: NA. The data after remove seasonal effect is 7.353733 which equals to 7.4 minus 0.0462673611.

Plot

plot(NJ_ts)
lines(seasadj_decomp_NJ, col = "red")

Explain: same as previous show that seasonality do small in the data so there is no significant effect when we remove the seasonal effect.

Do the forecast for data remove seasonal effect

fc_seas_NJ = forecast(seasadj_decomp_NJ, h = 12) ## forecast next year without seasonal effect
fc_seas_NJ

Plot the forecast

plot(fc_seas_NJ)

Explain: We can see from the chart that the forecast is relatively smooth compared to previous chart since we have remove the seasonal effect from the data.

Plot the decomp_NJ and its forecast

plot(decomp_NJ$x)

plot(forecast(decomp_NJ$x))

Explain: forecast looks the same as the latest observation is because we use the data without trend, seasonality, and random.

See the accuracy with other model

accuracy(fc_seas_NJ)
##                        ME      RMSE       MAE        MPE     MAPE       MASE
## Training set -0.001412008 0.1227902 0.0906283 0.04593622 1.809534 0.07436168
##                      ACF1
## Training set -0.001390668
HW_NJ = HoltWinters((NJ_ts))
accuracy(forecast(HW_NJ))
##                      ME      RMSE       MAE       MPE     MAPE     MASE
## Training set 0.02031734 0.2545643 0.1716999 0.7834687 3.945085 0.140882
##                  ACF1
## Training set 0.033303
ETS_NJ = ets(NJ_ts)
accuracy(forecast(ETS_NJ))
##                        ME      RMSE        MAE       MPE     MAPE       MASE
## Training set -0.003198643 0.1328658 0.09178555 0.0218789 1.798708 0.07531122
##                     ACF1
## Training set -0.01752757

Explain: We can tell from the RMSE numbers that the forecast of removing seasonal effect from data is the best fitted model since the number is the lowest.
